titleEn: Pūrṇamadaḥ: the unseen is whole, this world is whole — take one from the other and nothing is lost.
sanskrit: ॐ पूर्णमदः पूर्णमिदं पूर्णात्पूर्णमुदच्यते । पूर्णस्य पूर्णमादाय पूर्णमेवावशिष्यते ॥
transliteration: oṃ pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idaṃ pūrṇāt pūrṇam udacyate · pūrṇasya pūrṇam ādāya pūrṇam evāvaśiṣyate
meaningEn: That is whole; this is whole. From the whole, the whole comes forth. Take the whole out of the whole — and the whole alone is left. 'That' is what cannot be seen; 'this' is the world in front of you. The verse says both are complete, and that nothing is lost when one comes out of the other.
meaningHi: वह पूरा है; यह पूरा है। पूरे से पूरा निकलता है। पूरे में से पूरा निकाल लो — तो भी पूरा ही बचता है। 'वह' जो दिखता नहीं; 'यह' सामने की दुनिया। श्लोक कहता है दोनों पूरे हैं, और एक से दूसरा निकलने पर कुछ घटता नहीं।
sayItLike: Om poor-nam a-dah poor-nam i-dam · poor-naat poor-nam u-dach-ya-te · poor-nas-ya poor-nam aa-daa-ya · poor-nam e-vaa-va-shish-ya-te

words.glossEn: that — the far one, what is not seen
words.glossHi: वह — दूर वाला, जो दिखता नहीं
words.grammar: 'that' (over there) — the Upaniṣads use it for Brahman, the unseen

words.glossEn: this — the near one, the world here
words.glossHi: यह — पास वाला, सामने की दुनिया

words.grammar: is-raised — passive; the whole comes out of the whole
having-taken — a gerund; 'taking the whole of the whole'
stresses the word before it: 'the whole, and only the whole'
is-left — passive; eva + avaśiṣyate join as evāvaśiṣyate

source.ref: 5.1.1; the same verse is the peace-chant (śānti-pāṭha) of the Īśa Upaniṣad
source.note: 'That' and 'this' are the Upaniṣad's own words; the reading 'that = the unseen Brahman, this = the world' is the standard commentary (Śaṅkara) and is how the verse has been chanted for a thousand years.

significance.textSays: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 5.1.1: 'oṃ — that is whole, this is whole; from the whole the whole comes forth; taking the whole of the whole, the whole alone remains.'
significance.traditionSays: Chanted before and after Upaniṣad study and at the close of Vedāntic satsaṅg, followed by oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ; loved as the one verse that says the world and its source are both complete.
significance.weDoNotClaim: Any effect. It is a statement about reality, chanted as peace; it is quoted here and left to stand.

practice.timeOfDay: before and after study, or at the close of a gathering

quiz.prompt: In the verse, अदः (adaḥ, 'that') and इदम् (idam, 'this') point to —
options: the unseen and the world in front of you
